# Decision Trees for Classification

::: {.callout-note title="Connection with the theoretical volume"}
The mathematical treatment of entropy, impurity, recursive partitions, and decision trees is developed in Chapters 3, 6, and 13 of *Mathematical Foundations of Machine Learning* [@rodriguez2026fundamentos].
:::

## Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter, the reader will be able to:

- explain how a decision tree recursively partitions predictor space;
- calculate and interpret Gini impurity;
- distinguish tree growth, complexity control, and pruning;
- select model complexity using cross-validation within the training data;
- interpret rules and variable importance without confusing prediction with causation;
- evaluate a tree using a confusion matrix, sensitivity, specificity, and balanced accuracy;
- apply the method to ATUS and to an educational COVID-19 route.

## Basic idea

A decision tree classifies observations through a sequence of **if-then** questions. At each internal node, the algorithm selects a predictor and a split that produces child nodes with lower class impurity [@breiman1984classification].

Unlike k-NN, a decision tree does not require standardization because its decisions are based on predictor-specific splits rather than a common Euclidean distance.

## Gini impurity

A common impurity measure is

$$
Gini(t)=1-\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_{k,t}^2,
$$

where $p_{k,t}$ is the proportion of observations from class $k$ in node $t$.

For a binary node with proportions $p$ and $1-p$,

$$
Gini=1-p^2-(1-p)^2.
$$

```{r decision-tree-gini-en}
gini <- function(class_value) {
  p <- prop.table(table(class_value))
  1 - sum(p^2)
}

gini(c("A", "A", "A", "B", "B"))
gini(c("A", "A", "A", "A", "A"))
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Interpretation"}
A pure node has Gini impurity equal to zero. A useful split reduces the weighted impurity of the child nodes relative to the parent node.
:::

## Entropy and information gain

Another family of tree methods uses entropy,

$$
H(t)=-\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_{k,t}\log_2(p_{k,t}),
$$

and seeks splits with high information gain. ID3 and related algorithms popularized this approach [@quinlan1986induction]. In this chapter we use CART through `rpart`; classification trees are commonly grown using Gini-based splitting.

## Overfitting and pruning

A deep tree can fit training observations extremely well while generalizing poorly. CART can first grow a flexible tree and then **prune** it using a complexity parameter, `cp`.

::: {.callout-important title="The test set is not used for pruning"}
Complexity is selected using `rpart`'s internal cross-validation on the training data. The test set remains untouched until final evaluation.
:::

## Helper functions

```{r decision-tree-helpers-en}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(rpart)
source("../util_graficas.R")

stratified_train_test <- function(y, prop_train = 0.80, seed = 2026) {
  set.seed(seed)
  y <- factor(y)
  idx_train <- integer(0)

  for (class_value in levels(y)) {
    ids <- sample(which(y == class_value))
    n_train <- floor(prop_train * length(ids))
    idx_train <- c(idx_train, ids[seq_len(n_train)])
  }

  idx_train <- sort(idx_train)
  list(
    train = idx_train,
    test = setdiff(seq_along(y), idx_train)
  )
}

tree_metrics <- function(actual, predicted, positive, negative) {
  actual <- factor(actual, levels = c(positive, negative))
  predicted <- factor(predicted, levels = c(positive, negative))
  m <- table(Actual = actual, Predicted = predicted)

  TP <- m[positive, positive]
  FN <- m[positive, negative]
  FP <- m[negative, positive]
  TN <- m[negative, negative]

  safe_divide <- function(a, b) if (b == 0) NA_real_ else a / b
  sensitivity <- safe_divide(TP, TP + FN)
  specificity <- safe_divide(TN, TN + FP)

  list(
    confusion = m,
    metrics = data.frame(
      accuracy = safe_divide(TP + TN, sum(m)),
      sensitivity = sensitivity,
      specificity = specificity,
      balanced_accuracy = mean(c(sensitivity, specificity), na.rm = TRUE)
    )
  )
}
```

# Applied Case A: ATUS

## Load and prepare the data

To keep book rendering reproducible and reasonably fast, we use a sample of up to 20,000 records. A full applied analysis may use the complete dataset when computational resources permit.

```{r prepare-decision-tree-atus-en}
atus_path <- "../datos/atus_ml_preparado.csv"

if (!file.exists(atus_path)) {
  stop("../datos/atus_ml_preparado.csv was not found. Run Chapter 2 first.")
}

atus_ml <- read_csv(atus_path, show_col_types = FALSE)

set.seed(2026)
atus_tree_base <- atus_ml |>
  mutate(
    accident_class = factor(
      accidente_con_victimas,
      levels = c("Con víctimas", "Solo daños"),
      labels = c("With casualties", "Property damage only")
    ),
    MES = as.factor(MES),
    HOUR_NUM = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(ID_HORA)),
    HOUR_NUM = ifelse(
      HOUR_NUM >= 0 & HOUR_NUM <= 23,
      HOUR_NUM,
      NA_real_
    ),
    DIASEMANA = as.factor(DIASEMANA),
    TIPACCID = as.factor(TIPACCID),
    CAUSAACCI = as.factor(CAUSAACCI)
  ) |>
  drop_na(
    accident_class,
    MES,
    HOUR_NUM,
    DIASEMANA,
    TIPACCID,
    CAUSAACCI
  ) |>
  slice_sample(n = min(20000, n()))

data.frame(
  rows = nrow(atus_tree_base),
  columns = ncol(atus_tree_base)
)
```

## Stratified training-test split

```{r split-decision-tree-atus-en}
parts_atus <- stratified_train_test(
  atus_tree_base$accident_class,
  prop_train = 0.80,
  seed = 2026
)

train <- atus_tree_base[parts_atus$train, ]
test <- atus_tree_base[parts_atus$test, ]

rbind(
  training = prop.table(table(train$accident_class)),
  test = prop.table(table(test$accident_class))
)
```

## Grow a tree and study complexity

The initial tree is allowed to be relatively flexible. Its complexity table uses internal cross-validation to estimate `xerror`.

```{r fit-large-tree-atus-en}
set.seed(2026)

large_tree <- rpart(
  accident_class ~
    MES + HOUR_NUM + DIASEMANA + TIPACCID + CAUSAACCI,
  data = train,
  method = "class",
  control = rpart.control(
    cp = 0.0005,
    minsplit = 120,
    minbucket = 40,
    maxdepth = 10,
    xval = 10
  )
)

printcp(large_tree)
```

## Prune using cross-validation error

```{r prune-tree-atus-en}
cp_table <- large_tree$cptable
best_row <- which.min(cp_table[, "xerror"])
best_cp <- cp_table[best_row, "CP"]

model_tree <- prune(
  large_tree,
  cp = best_cp
)

best_cp
```

::: {.callout-note title="The 1-SE rule"}
A more conservative alternative is to choose the smallest tree whose cross-validation error is within one standard error of the minimum. That rule often favors simpler models. Here we use the minimum `xerror` to keep the procedure transparent, but both approaches are worth comparing in formal projects.
:::

## Variable importance

```{r variable-importance-tree-atus-en}
importance <- model_tree$variable.importance

if (!is.null(importance)) {
  importance_df <- data.frame(
    variable = names(importance),
    importance = as.numeric(importance),
    row.names = NULL
  ) |>
    arrange(desc(importance))

  importance_df
}
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Predictive importance is not causation"}
A predictor may contribute strongly to tree splits without causing the outcome. Importance scores describe the fitted tree and may also favor predictors that offer many possible splits.
:::

## Optional tree visualization

```{r optional-tree-plot-en, eval=FALSE}
plot(model_tree, uniform = TRUE, margin = 0.1)
text(model_tree, use.n = TRUE, cex = 0.7)
```

The plot is left as optional code because a tree with many nodes can become difficult to read on a PDF page.

## Final test evaluation

```{r evaluate-tree-atus-en}
pred_tree <- predict(
  model_tree,
  newdata = test,
  type = "class"
)

result_atus <- tree_metrics(
  test$accident_class,
  pred_tree,
  positive = "With casualties",
  negative = "Property damage only"
)

result_atus$confusion
result_atus$metrics
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Interpretation"}
Under class imbalance, overall accuracy should be read together with sensitivity, specificity, and balanced accuracy. A tree that predicts the majority class almost all the time can appear accurate while detecting the minority class poorly.
:::

# Interactive laboratory: build a CART split

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
Change the predictor and split point to see how a rule partitions the `iris` data and how much it reduces Gini impurity.

```{shinylive-r}
#| standalone: true
#| viewerHeight: 720
#| components: [viewer]

library(shiny)

gini_lab <- function(class_value) {
  if (length(class_value) == 0) return(0)
  p <- prop.table(table(class_value))
  1 - sum(p^2)
}

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Interactive CART split explorer"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      selectInput(
        "variable",
        "Splitting variable",
        choices = c(
          "Petal length" = "Petal.Length",
          "Petal width" = "Petal.Width",
          "Sepal length" = "Sepal.Length",
          "Sepal width" = "Sepal.Width"
        ),
        selected = "Petal.Length"
      ),
      uiOutput("cut_control")
    ),
    mainPanel(
      plotOutput("plot", height = "420px"),
      tableOutput("summary"),
      textOutput("interpretation")
    )
  )
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$cut_control <- renderUI({
    x <- iris[[input$variable]]
    sliderInput(
      "cut",
      "Split point",
      min = floor(min(x) * 10) / 10,
      max = ceiling(max(x) * 10) / 10,
      value = median(x),
      step = 0.1
    )
  })

  split_data <- reactive({
    req(input$cut)
    x <- iris[[input$variable]]
    left <- x <= input$cut
    right <- !left

    parent_gini <- gini_lab(iris$Species)
    left_gini <- gini_lab(iris$Species[left])
    right_gini <- gini_lab(iris$Species[right])
    n <- nrow(iris)

    weighted_gini <-
      sum(left) / n * left_gini +
      sum(right) / n * right_gini

    list(
      x = x,
      left = left,
      right = right,
      parent_gini = parent_gini,
      left_gini = left_gini,
      right_gini = right_gini,
      weighted_gini = weighted_gini,
      gain = parent_gini - weighted_gini
    )
  })

  output$plot <- renderPlot({
    d <- split_data()
    species_code <- as.integer(iris$Species)

    plot(
      d$x,
      jitter(as.integer(iris$Species), amount = 0.08),
      pch = 19,
      col = species_code,
      xlab = input$variable,
      ylab = "Species",
      yaxt = "n",
      main = "Proposed split"
    )
    axis(2, at = 1:3, labels = levels(iris$Species))
    abline(v = input$cut, lwd = 3, lty = 2)
  })

  output$summary <- renderTable({
    d <- split_data()
    data.frame(
      Node = c("Parent", "Left", "Right", "Weighted split"),
      Observations = c(
        nrow(iris),
        sum(d$left),
        sum(d$right),
        nrow(iris)
      ),
      Gini = round(
        c(d$parent_gini, d$left_gini, d$right_gini, d$weighted_gini),
        4
      )
    )
  })

  output$interpretation <- renderText({
    d <- split_data()
    paste0(
      "The impurity reduction is ", round(d$gain, 4),
      ". A larger reduction indicates a more useful split."
    )
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
```
:::

# Applied Case B: decision tree with COVID-19

The same reproducible period-selection procedure used in previous chapters is retained here.

```{r select-covid-tree-period-en}
covid_counts <- read_csv(
  "../datos/covid19/procesados/conteo_casos_confirmados_2020_2025.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

covid_year <- covid_counts |>
  filter(ESTADO == "PROCESADO", !is.na(CASOS_CONFIRMADOS)) |>
  slice_max(CASOS_CONFIRMADOS, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  pull(ANIO)

covid_path <- file.path(
  "../datos/covid19/procesados",
  paste0("covid19_mexico_", covid_year, "_ml_preparado.csv.gz")
)

if (!file.exists(covid_path)) {
  stop("The COVID-19 dataset selected by the reproducible procedure was not found.")
}
```

## Prepare and split the educational sample

```{r prepare-covid-tree-en}
covid_tree <- read_csv(covid_path, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(
    MURIO, EDAD, NEUMONIA, DIABETES, HIPERTENSION,
    OBESIDAD, RENAL_CRONICA, NUM_COMORBILIDADES
  ) |>
  drop_na() |>
  mutate(
    outcome = factor(
      MURIO,
      levels = c(1, 0),
      labels = c("Recorded death", "No recorded death")
    )
  ) |>
  select(-MURIO)

set.seed(2026)
covid_tree <- covid_tree |>
  slice_sample(n = min(12000, n()))

parts_covid <- stratified_train_test(
  covid_tree$outcome,
  prop_train = 0.80,
  seed = 2026
)

covid_train <- covid_tree[parts_covid$train, ]
covid_test <- covid_tree[parts_covid$test, ]
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Educational use only"}
Rules discovered in this administrative sample describe patterns in the selected data. They must not be interpreted as clinical, diagnostic, or treatment rules.
:::

## Grow, prune, and evaluate the COVID-19 tree

```{r fit-covid-tree-en}
set.seed(2026)

large_covid_tree <- rpart(
  outcome ~ EDAD + NEUMONIA + DIABETES + HIPERTENSION +
    OBESIDAD + RENAL_CRONICA + NUM_COMORBILIDADES,
  data = covid_train,
  method = "class",
  control = rpart.control(
    cp = 0.0005,
    minsplit = 80,
    minbucket = 30,
    maxdepth = 8,
    xval = 10
  )
)

best_cp_covid <- large_covid_tree$cptable[
  which.min(large_covid_tree$cptable[, "xerror"]),
  "CP"
]

covid_model_tree <- prune(large_covid_tree, cp = best_cp_covid)
best_cp_covid
```

```{r evaluate-covid-tree-en}
pred_covid_tree <- predict(
  covid_model_tree,
  covid_test,
  type = "class"
)

result_covid <- tree_metrics(
  covid_test$outcome,
  pred_covid_tree,
  positive = "Recorded death",
  negative = "No recorded death"
)

result_covid$confusion
result_covid$metrics
```

## Chapter summary

Decision trees turn classification into visible, flexible rules. Interpretability does not eliminate overfitting: depth and complexity should be controlled using training data and cross-validation, while the test set is reserved for final evaluation. The instability of a single tree motivates the next chapter, **Random Forest**, which combines many trees to reduce variance.

## Fundamental references

CART was systematically developed by @breiman1984classification. Information-gain tree induction was developed by @quinlan1986induction. A contemporary statistical-learning introduction can be found in @james2021islr.
